inputs.wacc_rationale: USD flows. Cost of equity = 10-yr UST ~4.2% + 0.7 beta x 5.0% ERP = 7.7%, rounded up to 8.0% because the listed Class A beta (~0.5-0.6, thin float, Hagen-family Class B control) understates the fundamental risk of a single-customer fee stream. No borrowings, so WACC = cost of equity. Fee-rate, litigation and Exchange-surplus risks are charged once, in the scenario paths and weights, never as a WACC premium and never per scenario. UNCHANGED in the 2026-11-19 update.

inputs.notes: MODEL CHOICE: routed to the owner-FCF component DCF (SKILL.md operating-company row), NOT the insurer BVPS-compounding row -- same model as the 2026-09-28 build. Indemnity is the attorney-in-fact of Erie Insurance Exchange and earns a 25%-of-written-premium management fee; it carries no underwriting reserves, no policyholder float and no investment-risk mandate -- the Exchange (owned by its subscribers, not by ERIE shareholders) holds all of that. Indemnity's value is a stream of fee cash flow with minimal capital intensity (capex ~3% of revenue, ROE ~25%), which is exactly what the owner-FCF engine discounts; a book-value model would capitalise a $2.55B equity base that is mostly an incidental investment portfolio and would miss the fee franchise. historical_growth.growth_rate_source: forward: Exchange direct-written-premium growth. FY2026 tracking ~1.7% total revenue (9M +1.8%; management fee revenue +3.8%, pass-through reimbursement revenue -6.2%) and mean-reverting to ~5% nominal P&C premium growth by FY2028 as new products (Erie Secure Auto in 10 states, Business Auto 2.0) and the new quoting platform lift new business; not a trailing CAGR.
historical_growth.growth_divergence_warning: Equity 5-yr CAGR 14.0% vs revenue 9.9% (+41%) and vs owner-FCF 13.8%: retained earnings compound faster than the fee base because the payout ratio is ~45%. Every FY2020-25 CAGR embeds the FY2023-24 hard-market rate surge (revenue +15.1% and +16.1%) that has already decayed to +7.2% in FY2025 and +1.8% in 9M-2026; none of them is a forward rate.
historical_growth.notes: All CAGRs on the FY2015-present Indemnity-standalone series (FY2020 -> FY2025 for 5-yr, FY2022 -> FY2025 for 3-yr); FY2008-2014 rows are consolidated with the Exchange and excluded. Unchanged from the 2026-09-28 build because no fiscal year has closed since. Owner-FCF series = reported FCF less investment income (SBC is zero): FY2020 254.2, FY2022 298.3, FY2025 486.1. The owner-FCF CAGR (13.8%) sits below the reported-FCF CAGR (14.7%) because investment income grew from 32.9 to 84.9 with rates, not because of SBC. Reported FCF also carries lumpy pension contributions (80.1 FY2018, 96.2 FY2023, 42.3 FY2025, and a further step-up in 9M-2026) which depress the earlier base and flatter the 3-yr rate.

base.growth_rationale: FY2026 +1.7% on nine-month actual +1.8% and a Q3 exit rate near zero for total revenue (fee revenue +2.6%, pass-through reimbursements -8.4%); FY2027 +3.0% from a ~2% written-premium run-rate with policies in force still shrinking; FY2028-30 recovers to 5-5.5% as Exchange premium growth normalises with new-product rollouts and improved quoting conversion; fades to 3% terminal.
base.margin_rationale: FY2025 EBITDA margin 19.3% (operating income 717.2 + D&A 69.5); nine months of FY2026 at 20.2% against 19.6% a year earlier, with Q4 seasonally the weakest quarter, puts the full year near 19.8%. Held flat at 19.8% for two more years and allowed only to 20.0% thereafter: the fee is capped at 25% so revenue cannot outrun premium, agent incentive and technology costs are rising, and AI/quoting efficiencies are the only source of expansion.
base.capex_rationale: Capex 2.8% FY2025 and 3.4% in 9M-2026 (technology modernisation); tapers to 2.2% as the programme completes, with D&A already at ~2.0% and settling at 2.1%. wc_capture -5%: receivables from the Exchange grow with fee revenue (FY2025 +28.5M on +272M revenue), partly offset by deferred-revenue and accrued-commission inflows.

scenario_narratives.base: The fee rate stays at the 25% ceiling (reset each December; held there every year since the mid-2000s) and the Stephenson/Barnett subscriber litigation, now back in Pennsylvania state court with an amended complaint covering 2020 to the present, grinds on without changing fee-setting governance. The interim-CEO period ends with an internal or like-minded appointment and no change of strategy. The Exchange's underwriting turnaround (combined ratio 100.6% in Q3-2026 vs 113.7% a year earlier) rebuilds surplus, but growth gets worse before it gets better: FY2026 total revenue is up only ~1.7% and FY2027 ~3% because policies in force are falling ~2% and retention is 87.2%, before premium growth recovers toward ~5% nominal from FY2028 as Erie Secure Auto, Business Auto 2.0 and the new quoting platform restore unit growth. Margins hold near 19.8-20%: shrinking pass-through revenue flatters the ratio while agent incentive and technology costs absorb the operating leverage. Ten-year horizon because the growth path is what is being judged, not a margin ramp; the year-1 owner-FCF margin (~12.5%) sits above the trailing-twelve-month actual (11.1%), the gap being pension-contribution, agent-incentive-payment and tax-payment timing.
scenario_narratives.bull: The Exchange returns to sub-100% combined ratios, surplus growth lets it price for share again, retention recovers above 90% and the product rollouts lift policies in force -- premium growth re-accelerates to 5% in FY2027 and 7% in FY2028-29 as the P&C cycle firms. AI-assisted subrogation, claims backlog reduction and the doubled quoting conversion push EBITDA margin to 21.5%. A permanent CEO is named quickly, the litigation is resolved without a fee-rate change and the December fee resets keep 25%. Same 8% WACC and 20x cap as base: the upside is operational, not a cheaper discount rate.
scenario_narratives.bear: The single-lever risk materialises: after another record catastrophe year or an adverse ruling in the state-court fiduciary action the board resets the fee to ~24% for FY2028 to protect Exchange surplus, taking ~4% off revenue in one step (-3% modelled for year 3) while the cost base does not shrink, so EBITDA margin drops to 16% and only partly recovers. Before that, FY2027 growth stalls at 1% and agent incentive costs take the margin to 18.5% as the Exchange pays more to hold a shrinking book through a leadership vacuum. Policies in force keep declining and retention stays below 88%, holding growth at ~2.5% thereafter. Terminal growth 2.5% and a 16x cap for a structurally slower franchise with an open governance question. Weighted at 30% -- above the 15% house default -- because the revenue stream depends on one customer and one discretionary board decision, and the litigation attacking exactly that decision is live.

probability_weighted.weights_rationale: Unchanged from the 2026-09-28 build. Bear held at 30% (house default 15%) for single-customer dependency on the Exchange, a discretionary fee rate revisited every December, and active subscriber litigation (Stephenson/Barnett, back in state court after the Supreme Court denied certiorari, amended to cover 2020 to the present) that targets the fee-setting practice itself; the accelerated CEO departure in November 2026 adds execution risk that this elevated weight already covers. Bull held at 20% because it needs three independent things -- a durable Exchange underwriting recovery, a return to unit growth against national direct writers, and a litigation outcome that leaves governance untouched -- to go right together. Base 50%.

valuation_philosophy.summary: Erie Indemnity is valued as what it is: a capital-light management-fee franchise whose cash flows are a fixed 25% slice of a mutual-like insurer's written premium. The owner-FCF build strips the investment income on its $1.95B portfolio (added back once at the bridge), charges no SBC because there is none, holds the share count flat because Erie neither issues nor repurchases, and discounts at an 8% USD cost of equity with all business-specific risk carried in the scenario paths and a 30% bear weight rather than a WACC premium. Terminal value is capped at 20x FCF (base/bull) and 16x (bear) even though the market has historically paid 25-35x earnings for this stock, so the model does not rely on the historical premium multiple persisting. The cap binds in all three scenarios.
key_risks_to_valuation: Fee-rate reset below 25%: each 1pt cut removes ~4% of revenue with no offsetting cost lever (bear case mechanism). The FY2027 rate is decided in December 2026.
Subscriber fiduciary-duty litigation (Stephenson/Barnett, Pennsylvania state court, amended to cover 2020 to the present) could force damages or a change in how the fee is set.

Exchange premium growth: policies in force -1.9% YoY and retention 87.2% in Q3-2026, written premium growth down to +1.8% -- if rate increases fade before unit growth returns, the FY2028-30 recovery to 5-5.5% in the base path does not happen.

Leadership: the CEO retired on 2 November 2026, two months ahead of plan, and the General Counsel is interim CEO during simultaneous product and technology rollouts; a permanent appointment has not been announced.
Agent incentive costs (+96.6M over nine months) growing faster than fee revenue would erode the 19.8-20% margin the base case holds.
Catastrophe and social-inflation losses at the Exchange erode surplus and pressure the fee decision even though they never touch Indemnity's own P&L.
Capex programme runs longer than modelled (3.4% of revenue in 9M-2026 vs 2.2% terminal), compressing FCF conversion.

Trailing-twelve-month owner FCF (458.6) is below the year-1 build (~517): if the larger pension contributions and agent incentive payments prove recurring rather than timing, base FCF is overstated by up to ~10%.
The Q4-2025 ~$102M non-operating charge is treated as one-off; if it recurs (e.g. a standing foundation commitment) base FCF is overstated by ~2%/yr.
